prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I Did, till we loved? Were we not weaned till then? But sucked on country pleasures, childishly? Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den? ’Twas so; but this, all pleasures fancies be. If ever any beauty I did see, Which I desired, and got, ’twas but a dream of thee. And now good-morrow to our waking souls, Which watch not one another out of fear; For love, all love of other sights controls, And makes one little room an everywhere. Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone, Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown, Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one. My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears, And true plain hearts do in the faces rest; Where can we find two better hemispheres, Without sharp north, without declining west? Whatever dies, was not mixed equally; If our two loves be one, or, thou and I Love so alike, that none do slacken, none can die.

Here is an elegant and professional prose adaptation of John Donne’s classic poem, *The Good-Morrow*, retaining every original thought, metaphor, and detail:

***

I truly reflect upon what you and I could have possibly done before we fell in love. Were we not yet fully mature, indulging merely in simple, childish pleasures? Or were we effectively asleep, like the legendary Seven Sleepers? 

Indeed, it was so; yet compared to our present devotion, all former pleasures were mere illusions. Any beauty I previously beheld, desired, and attained was nothing more than a faint anticipation of you.

And now, I bid welcome to our awakening souls, which gaze upon each other free from fear or mistrust. For true love transcends the desire for all other sights, transforming our single modest room into the entire universe. Let maritime explorers venture to new lands, and let cartographers reveal worlds upon worlds to others; let us instead possess our own shared world, wherein each of us embodies a complete universe and possesses the other.

My image is reflected in your eyes, as yours is in mine, revealing the sincere and earnest hearts within us. Where could one ever find two superior hemispheres—free from the bitter cold of the north and the fading light of the setting west? 

Anything that perishes does so because its elements were improperly balanced. If our two loves are truly united as one—or if you and I love each other with such perfect equality that neither affection wanes—then our love can never die.

***

**The Transcendent Power of True Love**

Looking back on the time before true love, life appears as little more than an unconscious, slumbering childhood. Prior to this profound awakening, all past pleasures, desires, and experiences were not genuine fulfillments, but merely vague premonitions and shadowy reflections of the partner who was yet to come. Life before this love was an unawakened state, waiting for reality to begin.

When mutual love finally ignites, it triggers a total transformation of the lovers' inner and outer worlds. The anxieties, suspicions, and fears that often govern human relationships are instantly replaced by an abiding, absolute trust. Under the influence of this devotion, even their immediate physical surroundings are redefined: the modest, shared room they inhabit ceases to be a confined space and expands, in their shared consciousness, into an entire universe. 

Because their love constitutes a complete cosmos, the lovers feel no impulse to explore the wider physical world. While discoverers and travelers venture across oceans to chart new lands, the lovers remain entirely content in their stillness. Their mutual devotion creates a self-contained existence so rich and whole that external globes and distant horizons become utterly redundant; to possess one another is to possess everything.

This grand, cosmic connection is anchored in profound intimacy. When the lovers gaze into each other’s eyes, they see a clear reflection of their own pure sincerity, unmarred by deceit or hesitation. Their two hearts beat in such seamless alignment that their bond remains entirely free from the friction, conflict, and decay that typically erode human relationships over time. 

Ultimately, it is this perfect balance and undivided unity that elevates their connection into the realm of the eternal. In the natural world, things deteriorate only when their elements are mismatched or out of harmony. Because the lovers' affection is perfectly mirrored and fused into a single indivisible whole, their bond transcends the frailties of the mortal condition. Their love, existing in flawless equilibrium, cannot falter, fade, or die.
outputs.L4:
Before this profound awakening, our lives were nothing more than a prelude—a long, unremembered infancy in which we drifted aimlessly through a world of shadows. Looking back on that former time, it seems as though we were like children not yet weaned from the simple, physical pleasures of existence, or like the legendary Seven Sleepers sealed away in a dark cave, utterly oblivious to the vibrant reality waiting outside. Every joy pursued before this moment was a mere illusion, a hollow phantom of the truth we now inhabit. If ever I lusted after or possessed beauty in those forgotten days, it was not the genuine article, but merely a fleeting, prophetic dream of you.

Now, at last, we bid a joyful and solemn welcome to our waking souls. As we open our eyes to one another, the watchfulness born of fear and insecurity vanishes entirely. True love has no need to look outward with suspicion; instead, it possesses a quiet, self-contained confidence that makes all other sights redundant. Let the ambitious explorers sail across uncharted oceans to map distant lands and discover new hemispheres. Let them claim vast territories for their kings and empires. For us, such grand endeavors are meaningless. In the sanctuary of this room, our mutual devotion contracts the entire cosmos into a single, sacred point. We have no need for the world outside, for each of us is a world unto ourselves, and together, our shared space becomes an all-encompassing universe.

When I gaze into your eyes, I see my own face reflected back at me, just as you see yours in mine. In this sacred visual exchange, there is no deceit, no hidden shadow; our plain, true hearts rest openly in our faces, entirely exposed and entirely understood. Together, we form two perfect, complementary hemispheres, free from the harsh, freezing cold of a sharp northern winter or the declining light of a setting western sun. Unlike the physical world, which is constantly fractured by change, storm, and distance, our spiritual landscape is whole and constant.

It is a fundamental law of nature that whatever perishes must first suffer from an imbalance—a clash of unequal elements that causes the whole to decay. But our love is subject to no such corruption. Because our devotion is perfectly equal, blended so seamlessly that neither of us loves more or less than the other, there is no internal strife to tear us apart. If my love matches yours so precisely that neither can ever slacken or fail, then our bond transcends the mortal realm. Bound by this harmonious, unyielding symmetry, our union is rendered immune to the ravages of time, destined to endure beyond decay and death itself.
outputs.L5:
The old summer house stood at the edge of the whispering pine forest, a place where the shadows **were** always longer and cooler than anywhere else. In those days, we spent endless afternoons wandering down the overgrown, sun-dappled paths, convinced that the woods held secrets reserved strictly for us. The days **were** slow, stretched out by the humid heat and the quiet innocence of youth. 

Looking back, I often wonder how much of that magic was real and how much was just the romanticism of memory. **Did** we actually hear music drifting from the abandoned gazebo on those windless nights, or was it merely the rustle of leaves filling the silence? **Did** time truly stop during those three golden months, or did we simply refuse to look at a clock? 

Decades have passed since then, and the old house has long been reclaimed by nature. **But** the memory of those moments remains untarnished. The wooden porch may have collapsed and the paths vanished under thick foliage, **but** whenever the cool autumn breeze strikes just right, I am carried instantly back to the edge of those woods, listening for a music that never really ended.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a classic Renaissance love poem that uses geographic and cosmological metaphors to describe two lovers forming their own world.
counterfactuals.output:
The absolute epitome of this theme is **"The Good-Morrow"** by the English Renaissance poet **John Donne** (published in 1633). 

Written during the Age of Discovery, Donne uses the dramatic geographic explorations and cosmological theories of his time to argue that the physical world of maps, hemispheres, and sea-captains pales in comparison to the self-contained world he and his lover create together.

***

### **The Good-Morrow**
*by John Donne*

I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I
Did, till we loved? Were we not weaned till then?
But sucked on country pleasures, childishly?
Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den?
’Twas so; but this, all pleasures fancies be.
If ever any beauty I did see,
Which I desired, and got, ’twas but a dream of thee.

And now good-morrow to our waking souls,
Which watch not one another out of fear;
For love, all love of other sights controls,
And makes one little room an everywhere.
Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone,
Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown,
Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one.

My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears,
And true plain hearts do in the faces rest;
Where can we find two better hemispheres,
Without sharp north, without declining west?
Whatever dies, was not mixed equally;
If our two loves be one, or, thou and I
Love so alike, that none do slacken, none can die.

***

### Why this poem fits your request:

* **Making "one little room an everywhere":** Donne captures the metaphysical idea that true love collapses space. The lovers' bedroom becomes the entirety of the cosmos.
* **Geographic Exploration:** In the second stanza, he references the Age of Discovery ("sea-discoverers" and "maps"). He suggests that while explorers sail off to chart physical lands, he and his beloved possess a far superior "world."
* **The Two Hemispheres:** In the final stanza, Donne looks into his lover's eyes and sees his reflection, viewing their two faces as two matching half-globes ("hemispheres"). Crucially, their world is better than the physical Earth because it has no "sharp north" (coldness/hardship) and no "declining west" (sunset/death).
